findings.requirement: Evidence of business cost or consequence
missingEvidence: Buyer correspondence for P-13's six lost bids — EV-011 carries the owner's recorded reasons, not the buyer's words, and two of the six record no reason at all.
Correspondence for won bids from all three owners, so that losses can be read against a denominator rather than in isolation.
Contract values for the four bids in EV-009, without which nothing can be said about the size of the consequence.
Any record of what distinguishes P-12's late submissions from P-11's and P-13's on-time ones, which is the question the conflict actually raises.
findings.rationale: CL-004 requires lateness to be established by the buyer rather than inferred, and the packet contains buyer statements pointing both ways. EV-009 meets the claim's standard exactly: four dated emails from four separate buyer organizations, each stating in the buyer's own words that the award was made before the proposal arrived, matched to send timestamps between 2 and 9 days past the stated deadline — roughly one per quarter over twelve months, for P-12. EV-010 contradicts it for P-11 with the same kind of material: five buyer emails covering every recorded loss in twelve months, all naming price or scope, three explicitly noting timely delivery, and zero bids submitted after a buyer deadline. EV-011 records for P-13 that all 13 proposals with a recorded deadline were sent before it, by a median of 6 days, with no loss attributed to timing. So the consequence is documented as occurring for one in-segment owner and documented as not occurring for two others. That is credible mixed evidence, not falsification: EV-009's four buyer emails are not weakened by the fact that other owners submit on time, and the claim is not disproved at its defined scope — it is shown to hold for some owners and not others. Averaging these into a single verdict would erase both the real consequence P-12 experiences and the real absence of it for P-11 and P-13. Note that EV-011 is weaker than the other two on the claim's own standard: it carries the owner's entered reasons rather than buyer correspondence, which is why it is recorded as conflicting rather than as decisive.
findings.impact: The consequence is real for at least one owner and demonstrably absent for two, which points away from a segment-wide cost story and toward a subset problem. Selling on recovered lost bids would overstate the value for the majority of owners in this packet. INT-003's reading — that late proposals cost owners about a contract a quarter — generalizes from the single owner it happens to be true for.
findings.recommendation: Stop testing whether the consequence exists and start testing who it happens to. Collect twelve months of bid correspondence from four further in-segment owners and record, alongside each loss, whether the owner submits before or after buyer deadlines and how many facilities they bid per month. Then check whether late submission tracks with proposal volume — P-12 has both the highest volume in the packet and the only documented lateness.
findings.verificationTest: Across twelve months of bid history from six independent in-segment owners, count owners with at least one buyer-stated late loss per quarter. If most owners show none, the claim does not hold at segment scope and should be rescoped to whichever subset it describes; if most show one or more, this finding moves to pass. Either result changes the finding.

definitionQuality.rationale: The claim names the consequence, the rate and the standard of proof, which is what makes the conflicting buyer statements comparable.

evidenceAssessment.rationale: One in-segment source meets the claim's standard of proof with buyer correspondence. Two other in-segment sources document the absence of the consequence over comparable periods, one with buyer correspondence and one with owner-entered records only.

contradictionAssessment.rationale: EV-010 is buyer correspondence of the same kind and quality as EV-009 and covers every loss in the period, showing the consequence did not occur for that owner. EV-011 records zero late submissions across 13 deadlines for a third owner. The conflict is between owners, not within any single record, and it does not falsify a claim that some owners lose bids this way.

findings.rationale: CL-005 asks for money or staff hours committed to the existing problem, sustained at least three consecutive months. EV-012 meets it plainly for P-12: eight consecutive monthly invoices at USD 250 with matching bank debits, an ongoing engagement, described as proposal drafting support. Two other in-segment sources conflict with it in different ways. EV-013 is a single record carrying both readings at once: P-11 did spend money on this problem — USD 198 across two charges for proposal software — and then cancelled after five weeks and four logins, with a contemporaneous written reason that the existing template was faster and that 'proposals aren't where my time goes'. That is a documented expenditure that falls short of the claim's three-month bar and an explicit statement that the problem did not warrant it. EV-014 shows P-13 evaluating a paid option in a documented thread and declining it on the reasoning that fourteen or fifteen bids a year cannot justify a monthly fee, with no purchase and no staff allocation appearing in twelve months of records. Under the fail conditions for this requirement, two in-segment sources declining or abandoning paid help with documented reasons would point to fail — but EV-012 is comparably documented commitment that is still running, so this is credible mixed evidence and the status is partial. The conflict is not noise to be resolved by counting: one owner pays every month, one paid and stopped, one considered and declined. Note that P-11's and P-13's stated reasons are their own words about their own decisions, which is the strongest form of stated reason available and still not an observed cause.
findings.impact: The packet contains conflicting observed commitment decisions: one owner sustains qualifying expenditure, one abandons it because the problem did not justify the expenditure, and one declines it on the same basis. Proposal volume may motivate a later hypothesis about variation, but it does not prove commitment, cause these decisions, or establish a segment-wide conclusion.
findings.recommendation: Collect documented proposal-related expense or staff-allocation records from three further independent in-segment owners. Proposal volume is optional context; if collected, align it to the commitment period and keep it non-contributing to REQ-5 status. Do not substitute demand or willingness to pay for the proposed product.
findings.verificationTest: For independent in-segment owners, classify only documented money or staff-hour commitment to the existing problem sustained for the defined period. Pass requires the configured minimum of qualifying commitment sources. Counterevidence requires a documented evaluation followed by decline or abandonment because the problem did not justify expenditure; non-purchase, missing records, unrelated budget constraints, and rejection of the proposed product do not qualify. Fail requires the configured counterevidence minimum with no comparably credible qualifying commitment within this packet; credible evidence on both sides remains partial.

definitionQuality.rationale: The claim names the qualifying resource types, a minimum duration, and scopes itself to the existing problem rather than the proposed product, so each source's behaviour can be sorted against it.

EV-013 additionally contains an internal conflict that must be preserved rather than resolved: money was spent on this problem, and it was withdrawn within five weeks.

findings.offSegmentSignal: EV-015 records USD 4,100 per month sustained for 22 months on a dedicated bid coordinator at P-14. It is by far the largest documented commitment in the packet and it is out of segment on headcount and on who produces proposals, so it neither supports nor weakens CL-005.
